newsitem.title: PERU: Peru takes hard line in crisis as hostages wilt.
newsitem.headline: Peru takes hard line in crisis as hostages wilt.

text.p: Peru's government refused on Friday to release jailed comrades of Marxist guerrillas who were holding nearly 400 hostages, many in worsening health, at the Japanese ambassador's residence for a third day.

"The situation inside is difficult. There is overcrowding, it is very hot," Red Cross official Sergio Natarajan said after visiting the residence with a doctor and a nurse. "Among the illnesses are diabetes, ulcers, heart problems and diarrhoea."

Red Cross officials are mediating between President Alberto Fujimori's government and about 20 rebels from the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) who stormed the residence on Tuesday night and took prisoner a glittering array of ministers, ambassadors and businessmen.
A sign was hoisted on Friday in a window of the besieged building pleading for water, electricity and telephones to be reconnected and agreeing to a news conference with Japanese television.
"There is no water, power or telephone. Reconnect." it read in Spanish.
Residents living near the Japanese ambassador's home say authorities have cut off power and water following the guerrilla takeover.
Peru's hard line led to differences with Japan, which indicated overnight it was "far apart in ideas" from Lima over how to handle the crisis.

Like other countries with nationals held inside the residence, Tokyo said saving the lives of the hostages -- who spent their third night sleeping on the floor in crumpled suits -- should be the top priority.
In the street outside the residence, family members clutched candles and prayed late into the night for their loved ones.
"There are 24 million Peruvians who will not allow the lives of those kidnapped to be threatened," said one of the vigil organisers, legislator Manuel Lajo.
Many homes in the capital and even in the provinces hoisted the Peruvian national flag as a show of support for the hostages' plight, local television images showed.

Initial talks with the rebels produced no apparent progress although four dazed hostages, one needing a wheelchair, were released late on Thursday, the first to be freed since about 100 women and elderly were let out in the hours after the assault.

Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda, who arrived on Thursday to help with negotiations, scheduled talks with mediators on Friday to try to find a way out of the plight but had no immediate plans to see Fujimori again following a brief first meeting on Thursday night.

Following that encounter, Tokyo signalled it was not happy with the Peruvian stance -- made clear in a statement early on Friday in which the government explicitly rejected "the demand to release any terrorists held in Peru's jails."
"Japan and Peru are far apart in ideas," government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama said in Japan. He did not elaborate on the problem, but said it was hampering progress toward a solution.
As the embassy residence is considered Japanese territory, international law requires Fujimori to seek Tokyo's approval for any assault.

So far, however, Lima's hard line with the guerrillas is playing well to local public opinion. Peruvians say they do not want to see the government cave in to the guerrillas' demands for the release of jailed comrades.
"The mere thought of all these people who are prisoners being set free scares me," one woman told a local radio station.

Fujimori ignored an ultimatum by the rebels to come and talk in person on Wednesday and has not made a public statement since the crisis began. However, in a letter U.S. President Bill Clinton sent on Thursday he said the safety of hostages would be his first priority in resolving the siege.

Canadian ambassador Anthony Vincent, released late on Wednesday with three other diplomats to mediate between rebels and authorities, said conditions in the residence, normally home to six people, were very cramped. "They're packed in," he said.

Hostages have survived on a meagre diet erratically provided by the Red Cross, which has also taken medical supplies and even chess sets and rosary chains into the residence. The organisation said 380 hostages were inside.

Governments worldwide have urged Peru not to use force and to do everything in its power to protect the hostages. Several countries, including the United States, have offered technical assistance to resolve the standoff.

The rebels assaulted the fortified compound from outside on Tuesday, linking up with comrades disguised as waiters at the cocktail reception to celebrate the Japanese Emperor's birthday, anti-terrorist police sources said. Cartridges were smuggled into the building beforehand among flowers and inside a Christmas cake.
The captives also include Peru's foreign minister, agriculture minister, supreme court president and the current and past chiefs of the anti-terrorism police.

Ecuador, which fought a brief border war with Peru early 1995, offered asylum to the rebels. "We can be of help, providing the Peruvian government asks for it," Ecuadoran President Abdala Bucaram said.
Attempts by the MRTA and the previously better-known Shining Path to overthrow the government have cost 30,000 lives and $25 billion in infrastructure damage since 1980.
